Summary: God binds Himself to His people with solemn promises, from Noah and Abraham through Moses and David to the new covenant in Christ's blood. Each covenant reveals more of His faithful character and His plan to bless the nations. In Jesus, every covenant promise finds its yes and its fulfilment.
KeyPassages: Genesis 15:17-21; Exodus 19:5-6; 2 Samuel 7:12-16; Jeremiah 31:31-34; Luke 22:20; Hebrews 8:6
RelatedBooks: Genesis; Exodus; 2 Samuel; Jeremiah; Luke; Hebrews
RelatedEvents: The Exodus and Crossing of the Red Sea; Last Supper; The Crucifixion

Summary: Redemption is God buying His people back at a price, first pictured when He ransomed Israel from slavery in Egypt. In the New Testament, Christ's blood redeems us from sin, and creation itself waits for final redemption. It is the story of a God who pays what we could never pay to make us His own.
KeyPassages: Exodus 6:6; Ruth 4:4-10; Psalm 130:7; Mark 10:45; Ephesians 1:7; Romans 8:23
RelatedBooks: Exodus; Ruth; Psalms; Mark; Ephesians; Romans
RelatedEvents: The Exodus and Crossing of the Red Sea; The Crucifixion; The Resurrection

Summary: From the first offerings in Genesis to the Passover lamb and the daily temple sacrifices, Scripture teaches that sin costs life and that God Himself provides the substitute. All those sacrifices point forward to Jesus, the Lamb of God who offered Himself once for all. Because His sacrifice is complete, we can draw near to God with confidence.
RelatedPeople: Abraham; Isaac; Aaron; Jesus; John the Baptist
RelatedEvents: Binding of Isaac; The Passover; The Crucifixion

Summary: God is utterly pure, set apart, and glorious, and He calls His people to be holy as He is holy. The tabernacle, the law, and the prophets all show both the beauty and the seriousness of His holiness. In Christ we are made holy and, by the Spirit, we grow in holiness day by day.
RelatedEvents: Giving of the Law at Sinai; Pentecost

Summary: Sin is humanity's rebellion against God, beginning with Adam and Eve and spreading to every heart, bringing death and brokenness to the world. Scripture never minimises sin, but it also never leaves us without hope. From Genesis 3:15 onward, God promises and provides a Saviour who defeats sin at the cross.
KeyPassages: Genesis 3:6-19; Psalm 51:5; Isaiah 59:2; Romans 3:23; Romans 6:23; 1 John 1:8-9
RelatedEvents: The Fall; David and Bathsheba; The Crucifixion

Summary: God loves justice and hates oppression, commanding His people to defend the widow, the orphan, the foreigner, and the poor. The prophets thundered against injustice when Israel grew comfortable and careless. At the cross, God's justice and mercy meet, and His coming kingdom will set every wrong right at last.
KeyPassages: Deuteronomy 16:20; Psalm 33:5; Isaiah 1:17; Amos 5:24; Micah 6:8; Romans 3:25-26
RelatedBooks: Deuteronomy; Psalms; Isaiah; Amos; Micah; Romans
RelatedEvents: Giving of the Law at Sinai; The Crucifixion

Summary: Mercy is God's compassion toward those who deserve judgment, shown when He spared Israel again and again and supremely when He gave His Son. Jesus embodied mercy, welcoming sinners, healing the broken, and forgiving even those who crucified Him. Because we have received mercy, we are called to be merciful to others.
KeyPassages: Exodus 34:6-7; Psalm 103:8-13; Micah 7:18; Luke 6:36; Ephesians 2:4-5; Titus 3:5
RelatedBooks: Exodus; Psalms; Micah; Luke; Ephesians; Titus
RelatedEvents: The Exodus and Crossing of the Red Sea; Jonah and the Great Fish; The Crucifixion

Summary: Salvation is God's rescue of sinners from sin, death, and judgment, accomplished by grace through faith in Jesus Christ. The Old Testament celebrates God as Saviour who delivers His people, and the New Testament proclaims that same salvation to all who believe. It is past, present, and future: we have been saved, are being saved, and will be saved.
KeyPassages: Exodus 14:13; Psalm 62:1; Isaiah 12:2; Luke 19:10; Acts 4:12; Ephesians 2:8-9
RelatedBooks: Exodus; Psalms; Isaiah; Luke; Acts; Ephesians
RelatedEvents: The Exodus and Crossing of the Red Sea; The Crucifixion; The Resurrection; Pentecost

Summary: Faith is trusting God and taking Him at His word, exemplified by Abraham who believed God and it was credited to him as righteousness. Hebrews 11 celebrates ordinary men and women who lived, suffered, and died trusting promises they had not yet seen fulfilled. Faith is not wishful thinking; it rests on the faithful character of God Himself.
KeyPassages: Genesis 15:6; Habakkuk 2:4; Hebrews 11:1; Hebrews 11:6; Romans 10:17; James 2:17
RelatedEvents: Binding of Isaac; Noah and the Flood; The Resurrection

Summary: Grace is God's undeserved favour freely given to sinners, the heartbeat of the gospel from beginning to end. We are justified by grace, sustained by grace, and taught by grace to say no to ungodliness and yes to godliness. Grace humbles the proud, lifts the lowly, and leaves no room for boasting except in Christ.
KeyPassages: Genesis 6:8; Psalm 84:11; John 1:16-17; Romans 5:20; Ephesians 2:8; Titus 2:11-12
RelatedBooks: Genesis; Psalms; John; Romans; Ephesians; Titus
RelatedEvents: The Crucifixion; Conversion of Saul (Paul); Pentecost

Summary: God is love, and His love is shown most clearly in giving His Son for us while we were still sinners. The great commandments sum up the whole law: love God with all your heart and love your neighbour as yourself. Love is the mark by which the world will know we belong to Jesus.
KeyPassages: Deuteronomy 6:5; Psalm 136:1; John 3:16; Romans 5:8; 1 Corinthians 13:4-7; 1 John 4:8-10
RelatedBooks: Deuteronomy; Psalms; John; Romans; 1 Corinthians; 1 John
RelatedEvents: The Crucifixion; Last Supper; Creation

Summary: Biblical hope is not wishful thinking but a confident expectation anchored in God's promises and in Christ's resurrection. It held Abraham, sustained Israel in exile, and carries believers through suffering today. Hebrews calls this hope an anchor for the soul, firm and secure — the anchor at the heart of this blog.
KeyPassages: Psalm 42:11; Jeremiah 29:11; Romans 5:3-5; Romans 15:13; Hebrews 6:19; 1 Peter 1:3
RelatedEvents: Fall of Jerusalem and the Exile; The Resurrection; Cyrus's Decree and Return from Exile

Summary: The Kingdom of God is God's righteous reign, promised in the Old Testament and announced by Jesus as near in His own ministry. It grows like a mustard seed, turns worldly values upside down, and will one day fill the earth when Christ returns. To seek first His kingdom is to live now by the values of the age to come.
KeyPassages: Daniel 2:44; Daniel 7:14; Mark 1:14-15; Matthew 6:33; Luke 17:20-21; Revelation 11:15
RelatedPeople: Daniel; Jesus; John the Baptist; Paul
RelatedEvents: Birth of Jesus; The Crucifixion; The Resurrection; Pentecost

Summary: Scripture opens with God speaking light into darkness, and that contrast runs through the whole Bible as a picture of good and evil, truth and falsehood, life and death. Jesus declared Himself the Light of the World, and His followers are called to shine as lights in a dark world. In the new creation, darkness will be gone forever.
KeyPassages: Genesis 1:3-4; Psalm 27:1; Isaiah 9:2; John 1:5; John 8:12; Ephesians 5:8; Revelation 22:5
RelatedBooks: Genesis; Psalms; Isaiah; John; Ephesians; Revelation
RelatedEvents: Creation; Birth of Jesus; The Crucifixion; The Resurrection

Summary: God reveals Himself as a Shepherd who seeks, feeds, guides, and protects His sheep, most tenderly in Psalm 23. Israel's leaders were meant to shepherd the flock, and when they failed, God promised to shepherd His people Himself. Jesus fulfils that promise as the Good Shepherd who lays down His life for the sheep.
KeyPassages: Genesis 49:24; Psalm 23:1; Psalm 80:1; Ezekiel 34:11-16; John 10:11-14; 1 Peter 5:4
RelatedEvents: David Becomes King; Birth of Jesus; The Crucifixion

Summary: In the Old Testament, Israel is God's vine, planted to bear fruit for the nations, yet often failing to do so. Jesus takes up the image, declaring Himself the true Vine and His disciples the branches who bear fruit only by abiding in Him. Fruitfulness flows from remaining in Christ, not from striving apart from Him.
RelatedEvents: The Exodus and Crossing of the Red Sea; Last Supper; Pentecost

Summary: The temple was the dwelling place of God's presence among Israel, the centre of worship, sacrifice, and prayer in Jerusalem. Jesus honoured the temple, cleansed it, and foretold its destruction, while pointing to His own body as the true temple. Now God's Spirit dwells in His church and in every believer, and the new creation needs no temple because the Lord Himself is there.
KeyPassages: Exodus 25:8; 1 Kings 8:27-30; Psalm 84:1-4; John 2:19-21; 1 Corinthians 3:16; Revelation 21:22
RelatedBooks: Exodus; 1 Kings; Psalms; John; 1 Corinthians; Revelation
RelatedEvents: Building of Solomon's Temple; Pentecost; Rebuilding of the Temple

Summary: God heard Israel's groaning in Egypt and delivered them with a mighty hand through Moses, the Passover, and the parting of the sea. The Exodus became Israel's defining story of salvation, retold at every Passover. The New Testament presents Jesus' work as the greater Exodus, delivering us from slavery to sin and death.
RelatedEvents: The Exodus and Crossing of the Red Sea; The Passover; The Crucifixion

Summary: Because of persistent idolatry, Israel and Judah were carried into exile, losing land, temple, and king, yet God did not abandon them there. Prophets like Jeremiah and Ezekiel spoke hope in exile, and under Cyrus God brought His people home to rebuild. The return was real but incomplete, pointing forward to the greater restoration Jesus brings.
KeyPassages: 2 Kings 25:21; Jeremiah 29:4-14; Ezekiel 37:1-14; Ezra 1:1-4; Psalm 137:1; Isaiah 40:1-11
RelatedBooks: 2 Kings; Jeremiah; Ezekiel; Ezra; Psalms; Isaiah
RelatedPeople: Jeremiah; Ezekiel; Daniel; Ezra; Nehemiah; Cyrus the Great
RelatedEvents: Fall of Jerusalem and the Exile; Cyrus's Decree and Return from Exile; Rebuilding of the Temple

Summary: Biblical wisdom is skill for living in God's world God's way, beginning with the fear of the Lord. Proverbs, Job, and Ecclesiastes explore work, speech, money, suffering, and the limits of human understanding. In the New Testament, Christ Himself becomes for us wisdom from God, wiser than Solomon and the answer to our deepest questions.
KeyPassages: Proverbs 1:7; Proverbs 3:5-6; Job 28:28; Ecclesiastes 12:13; James 1:5; 1 Corinthians 1:30
RelatedEvents: Building of Solomon's Temple; Birth of Jesus

Summary: Worship is God's people ascribing worth to Him in spirit and in truth, in song, prayer, obedience, and everyday life offered as a living sacrifice. From Abraham's altars to the Psalms to the heavenly throne room in Revelation, worship is heaven's activity breaking into earth. True worship centres on who God is and what He has done in Christ.
KeyPassages: Genesis 22:5; Psalm 95:6; Psalm 100:1-5; John 4:23-24; Romans 12:1; Revelation 5:12-13
RelatedEvents: Binding of Isaac; Building of Solomon's Temple; Pentecost

Summary: Prayer runs through Scripture as God's people cry out, intercede, give thanks, and listen — from Abraham pleading for Sodom to Hannah's tears to Daniel's open window. Jesus taught His disciples to pray to their Father with simple trust, and He Himself prayed through the night and on the cross. Because of Christ, we can approach God's throne of grace with confidence.
KeyPassages: Genesis 18:23-32; 1 Samuel 1:10-20; Psalm 66:19; Daniel 6:10; Matthew 6:9-13; Hebrews 4:16
RelatedBooks: Genesis; 1 Samuel; Psalms; Daniel; Matthew; Hebrews
RelatedEvents: Destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah; Daniel in the Lions' Den; The Crucifixion; Pentecost

Summary: Forgiveness is at the centre of God's dealings with us: Joseph forgave his brothers, David pleaded for pardon, and Jesus forgave sinners and prayed for His executioners. On the cross, God provided the basis on which sins can be fully and justly forgiven. Having been forgiven so much, we are commanded to forgive others from the heart.
KeyPassages: Genesis 50:15-21; Psalm 32:5; Psalm 103:12; Matthew 6:14-15; Luke 23:34; Ephesians 4:32; Colossians 3:13
RelatedBooks: Genesis; Psalms; Matthew; Luke; Ephesians; Colossians
RelatedEvents: Joseph Rises to Power in Egypt; The Crucifixion; Martyrdom of Stephen

Summary: The Bible ends where it began, only greater: a new heavens and new earth where God dwells with His people and wipes away every tear. That future has already broken in, for anyone in Christ is a new creation, raised to new life by the Spirit. New creation hope steadies us now and shapes how we care for God's world and one another.
KeyPassages: Genesis 1:31; Isaiah 65:17; 2 Corinthians 5:17; Galatians 6:15; Revelation 21:1-5; Romans 8:19-21
RelatedBooks: Genesis; Isaiah; 2 Corinthians; Galatians; Revelation; Romans
RelatedEvents: Creation; The Resurrection; Pentecost

Summary: Light in Scripture stands for God's truth, purity, guidance, and life, shining first at creation and finally in the face of Christ. Jesus, the Light of the World, exposes darkness, guides our steps, and calls His people the light of the world. Walking in the light means honest, joyful fellowship with God and one another.
KeyPassages: Genesis 1:3; Psalm 119:105; Isaiah 60:1; Matthew 5:14-16; John 8:12; 1 John 1:5-7
RelatedBooks: Genesis; Psalms; Isaiah; Matthew; John; 1 John
RelatedEvents: Creation; Birth of Jesus; Transfiguration

Summary: Water appears at creation, in the Flood, at the Red Sea, and in water from the rock, as a picture of both judgment and life-giving salvation. The prophets promised cleansing water and rivers in the desert, and Jesus offered living water that becomes a spring welling up to eternal life. Baptism unites believers with Christ, and Revelation ends with the river of the water of life.
KeyPassages: Genesis 1:2; Exodus 14:21-31; Exodus 17:6; Ezekiel 36:25; John 4:13-14; John 7:37-39; Revelation 22:1-2
RelatedPeople: Moses; Noah; Jesus; The Samaritan Woman
RelatedEvents: Creation; Noah and the Flood; The Exodus and Crossing of the Red Sea; Baptism of Jesus

Summary: Bread is God's daily provision, from manna in the wilderness to the prayer 'give us this day our daily bread.' Jesus multiplied loaves for hungry crowds and then declared, 'I am the Bread of Life,' giving His own body as food for the world. At His table we remember Him and are nourished by grace until He comes again.
KeyPassages: Exodus 16:4; Deuteronomy 8:3; Matthew 6:11; John 6:35; John 6:51; 1 Corinthians 11:23-26
RelatedEvents: Wilderness Wanderings; Feeding of the Five Thousand; Last Supper

Summary: The Lamb is one of Scripture's richest pictures of Christ: the Passover lamb whose blood sheltered Israel, the lamb provided on Mount Moriah, and Isaiah's suffering servant led like a lamb to the slaughter. John the Baptist announced Jesus as the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world. Revelation crowns the Lamb who was slain as worthy of all worship.
KeyPassages: Genesis 22:7-8; Exodus 12:3-13; Isaiah 53:7; John 1:29; 1 Peter 1:18-19; Revelation 5:12
RelatedBooks: Genesis; Exodus; Isaiah; John; 1 Peter; Revelation
RelatedPeople: Abraham; Isaac; Moses; Isaiah; Jesus; John the Baptist
RelatedEvents: Binding of Isaac; The Passover; The Crucifixion; The Resurrection

Summary: The cross is the centre of the Christian faith, where Jesus bore our sin, defeated the powers of evil, and reconciled us to God. What looked like shame and defeat, God turned into wisdom, power, and salvation for all who believe. Believers take up their cross daily, boasting only in the cross of Christ.
KeyPassages: Isaiah 53:4-6; Matthew 27:32-56; John 19:17-30; 1 Corinthians 1:18; Galatians 6:14; Colossians 2:14-15
RelatedBooks: Isaiah; Matthew; John; 1 Corinthians; Galatians; Colossians
RelatedPeople: Jesus; Mary, Mother of Jesus; Paul
RelatedEvents: The Crucifixion; Last Supper

Summary: Jesus' resurrection is the firstfruits of the new creation, God's public declaration that death does not have the last word. Believers share that life now, raised with Christ and empowered by the Spirit to walk in newness of life. One day our bodies too will be raised, imperishable, to share His glory forever.
KeyPassages: John 11:25-26; Romans 6:4-5; 1 Corinthians 15:20-22; Philippians 3:10-11; Colossians 3:1; 1 Peter 1:3
RelatedBooks: John; Romans; 1 Corinthians; Philippians; Colossians; 1 Peter
RelatedPeople: Jesus; Lazarus; Mary Magdalene; Paul; Peter
RelatedEvents: The Resurrection; Raising of Lazarus; Pentecost

Summary: Peace — shalom — is wholeness with God, with others, and within ourselves, lost in the Fall and restored through Christ who is our peace. Jesus gives a peace the world cannot give, guarding hearts and minds even in trouble. One day the Prince of Peace will reign, and swords will become ploughshares.
KeyPassages: Numbers 6:24-26; Isaiah 9:6; John 14:27; Romans 5:1; Ephesians 2:14; Philippians 4:7
RelatedBooks: Numbers; Isaiah; John; Romans; Ephesians; Philippians
RelatedEvents: Birth of Jesus; The Crucifixion; The Resurrection

Summary: Joy in Scripture is deeper than happiness, rooted in who God is and what He has done, so it can endure even in sorrow and suffering. The Psalms sing it, Jesus promised His joy to His disciples, and joy is a fruit of the Spirit in every believer. The joy of the Lord is our strength.
KeyPassages: Nehemiah 8:10; Psalm 16:11; Habakkuk 3:17-18; John 15:11; Philippians 4:4; Galatians 5:22
RelatedBooks: Nehemiah; Psalms; Habakkuk; John; Philippians; Galatians
RelatedEvents: Cyrus's Decree and Return from Exile; Birth of Jesus; The Resurrection; Pentecost

Summary: Patience reflects God's own character, for He is slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love toward a rebellious world. Abraham waited for a son, Joseph waited in prison, and God's people waited centuries for the Messiah, learning that God's timing is never wasted. The Spirit grows patience in us as we wait hopefully for Christ's return.
KeyPassages: Exodus 34:6; Psalm 40:1; Romans 8:25; Galatians 5:22; James 5:7-8; 2 Peter 3:9
RelatedBooks: Exodus; Psalms; Romans; Galatians; James; 2 Peter
RelatedEvents: Binding of Isaac; Joseph Sold into Egypt; Birth of Jesus

Summary: Greatness in God's kingdom is measured by service, a pattern set by Jesus who came not to be served but to serve and give His life as a ransom. Isaiah's Suffering Servant, the foot-washing in John 13, and Paul's teaching all call believers to humble, joyful service. The Servant King shows us that stooping to serve is the way up in His kingdom.
KeyPassages: Isaiah 42:1; Isaiah 53:11; Mark 10:43-45; John 13:14-15; Philippians 2:5-8; 1 Peter 4:10
RelatedEvents: The Exodus and Crossing of the Red Sea; Last Supper; The Crucifixion

Summary: God does not give sparingly. From manna in the wilderness to loaves multiplied for a crowd, Scripture shows a Father who provides more than enough, and His generosity is meant to overflow into generosity toward others. Abundance is never about storing up for ourselves, but about trusting the Giver and sharing what He has given.
RelatedEvents: Wilderness Wanderings; The Feeding of the Five Thousand

Summary: To be accepted is to be welcomed as you are, and that is exactly how God receives those who come to Him through Christ. Jesus welcomed sinners, outcasts, and strangers, and Paul urges believers to accept one another just as Christ accepted them. Christian acceptance never means approving everything, but it does mean no one is beyond the reach of God's welcome.
RelatedEvents: The Prodigal Son; Peter and Cornelius

Summary: Apostasy is the sober reality of turning away from the faith once embraced. Scripture warns plainly that some will abandon the truth, exchanging it for error or for the world's approval, and it calls believers to hold fast and to watch over one another. The warnings are given not to frighten the faithful, but to keep them faithful.
RelatedPeople: Paul; John the Apostle; Judas Iscariot
RelatedEvents: The Golden Calf; The Kingdom Divides

Summary: Belief is more than agreeing with an idea; it is trusting a Person. Scripture calls us to believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and to stake our lives on that truth. Such belief receives forgiveness, gives new life, and shows itself in obedience.
RelatedEvents: The Resurrection; Conversion of Saul (Paul)

Summary: Long before Jesus was born, Micah promised that a ruler would come from little Bethlehem, one whose origins are from ancient days. Matthew sees that promise fulfilled when Jesus is born in David's town, the shepherd-king who would rule not by force but by laying down His life. The smallness of Bethlehem is the point: God's greatest King came in the humblest way.
RelatedPeople: Jesus; Mary, Mother of Jesus; Joseph, Husband of Mary
RelatedEvents: The Birth of Jesus

Summary: At the threshold of the Promised Land, Moses set before Israel two paths: blessing for obedience and curse for rebellion. The choice was stark because the covenant was serious — God's people could not drift into faithfulness. Yet the story does not end with curse, for Christ bore the curse so that the blessing of Abraham might come to all who believe.
RelatedEvents: Giving of the Law at Sinai; Crossing the Jordan

Summary: Blessing is God's favor resting on His people, spoken over Abraham and extended to every nation through Christ. In the Old Testament it meant land, children, and God's presence; in the New Testament it reaches its fullness as every spiritual blessing in Christ. To be blessed is to live under God's kind hand, and to become a blessing to others.
RelatedEvents: The Call of Abraham; The Sermon on the Mount

Summary: Believers are not merely like-minded individuals; they are brothers and sisters, bound together as one family in Christ. Scripture urges them to love one another warmly, carry one another's burdens, and live at peace. True brotherhood shows the world what the Father's household looks like.
RelatedPeople: Jesus; Paul; John the Apostle; Joseph, Son of Jacob
RelatedEvents: Joseph and His Brothers; Pentecost

Summary: Character is who you are when no one is watching, and God shapes it slowly through trials, obedience, and time. Scripture links suffering to endurance, endurance to character, and character to hope. The goal is not a polished reputation but a life that quietly resembles Christ.
RelatedPeople: Paul; Simon Peter; Joseph, Son of Jacob
RelatedEvents: Joseph Rises to Power in Egypt; The Temptation in the Wilderness

Summary: Christ alone saves, because He alone is both God and man, both priest and sacrifice. No teacher, ritual, or good deed can stand beside Him; to add anything to Christ is to lose Christ. The church confesses Him as the only mediator between God and humanity, and the only name by which we are saved.
RelatedEvents: The Crucifixion; The Resurrection

Summary: Jesus did not only teach the way; He walked it. He washed feet, welcomed children, forgave enemies, and laid down His life, leaving His followers a pattern to follow. To follow His example is not to earn salvation but to live out the salvation He has given.
RelatedEvents: The Last Supper; The Crucifixion

Summary: The New Testament ends with a promise: Jesus will return, visibly and gloriously, to judge the world and make all things new. His first coming was in humility; His second will be in power, and every believer is called to live ready — watchful, faithful, and full of hope.
RelatedEvents: The Ascension; Transfiguration

Summary: Christian living is ordinary life offered to God: work, family, neighbors, and rest all shaped by the gospel. Paul sums it up as presenting our bodies as living sacrifices and being transformed by renewed minds. It is not perfection but direction — a life increasingly conformed to Christ.
RelatedEvents: The Sermon on the Mount; Pentecost

Summary: The church grows as the gospel spreads and believers are added to the fellowship. Acts shows growth through preaching, prayer, shared life, and suffering, never through human technique alone. Healthy growth is both numerical and spiritual: more disciples, and deeper ones.
RelatedEvents: Pentecost; Jerusalem Council

Summary: God is a God of order, and the church reflects His character when its life is ordered well — leaders qualified, worship decent, disputes handled with wisdom. Order is not cold bureaucracy; it is love given structure, so that the whole body can flourish and the gospel is not hindered.
RelatedEvents: Jerusalem Council; Pentecost

Summary: When Judah faced exile, Isaiah spoke comfort: her warfare is ended, her iniquity pardoned, and her God is coming. Comfort for Judah was never mere sympathy; it was the promise that God had not abandoned His people and would bring them home. That same comfort reaches all who mourn under judgment, pointing to Christ who bears our sorrows.
RelatedEvents: Fall of Jerusalem and the Exile; Cyrus's Decree and Return from Exile

Summary: Israel waited for a King who would reign in righteousness, and the prophets pictured Him riding humbly into Jerusalem. Jesus entered the city to acclaim, yet His crown would be thorns before it was glory. He is the Coming King who will return to reign forever, and His kingdom is already breaking into the world.
RelatedPeople: Jesus; King David; Zechariah the Prophet
RelatedEvents: Triumphal Entry; David Becomes King

Summary: God's compassion does not stop at Israel's borders. Jonah learned this reluctantly when God spared Nineveh, and Isaiah foresaw a Servant who would be a light to the nations. In Christ, that compassion reaches every tribe and tongue, and the church carries it to the ends of the earth.
RelatedEvents: Jonah and Nineveh; Pentecost

Summary: The conquest of Canaan was God's gift of the land He had promised, won not by Israel's strength but by His presence. Yet the conquest was incomplete, and the land itself pointed forward to a greater rest. The battles remind us that God's promises are sure, and that victory belongs to the Lord.
RelatedEvents: Crossing the Jordan; Fall of Jericho

Summary: To be consecrated is to be set apart for God's purposes, as Israel was called a holy nation and believers are called a holy priesthood. Consecration touches every part of life — body, work, worship — offered wholly to God. It is not withdrawal from the world but dedication within it.
RelatedEvents: Giving of the Law at Sinai; The Ten Commandments

Summary: Jude urges believers to contend for the faith once delivered, not with cruelty but with conviction. False teaching spreads quietly, so the church must know the truth well enough to recognize its counterfeits. Contending is an act of love: for God, for the church, and for those being led astray.
RelatedPeople: Paul; Simon Peter; John the Apostle
RelatedEvents: Jerusalem Council; Martyrdom of Stephen

Summary: Covenant love is God's steadfast, loyal love — the Hebrew hesed — that keeps His promises even when His people break theirs. It is love bound by oath, shown at Sinai, renewed through the prophets, and poured out fully in Christ. To know covenant love is to rest in a faithfulness that never lets go.
RelatedEvents: The Golden Calf; The Exodus and the Red Sea

Summary: Again and again God's people returned to renew their covenant: at Shechem under Joshua, under Josiah after the Law was found, and under Nehemiah after exile. Renewal meant hearing God's word, confessing failure, and recommitting to obey. Every generation needs its own renewal, for faith is never inherited automatically.
RelatedEvents: Ezra Reads the Law; Nehemiah Rebuilds the Wall

Summary: Israel's story is shadowed by unfaithfulness — idols, injustice, and forgotten vows. The prophets name it plainly: the people broke the covenant their God had kept. Yet even unfaithfulness becomes a stage for grace, as God disciplines, restores, and finally keeps the covenant Himself in Christ.
RelatedEvents: The Golden Calf; The Kingdom Divides

Summary: Judges tells a grim cycle: sin, oppression, crying out, deliverance, and sin again. Each round shows that Israel's problem was not bad leaders but a wandering heart. The cycle only breaks when a true King comes who can change hearts from within.
RelatedEvents: Deborah and Barak Defeat Sisera; Gideon's Victory over Midian

Summary: Faith is not only for crises; it is for Tuesday mornings. Daily faith means trusting God for today's bread, today's work, and today's obedience, one day at a time. The manna principle still holds: God gives enough for today, and tomorrow's grace arrives tomorrow.
RelatedEvents: The Sermon on the Mount; Wilderness Wanderings

Summary: From Ruth and Boaz through Jesse to David, and from David to Jesus, Scripture traces a family line held together by God's promise. The lineage includes outsiders, failures, and kings, showing that God's plan runs through real human history. Matthew opens his Gospel with this genealogy to announce: the promised King has arrived.
RelatedEvents: Story of Ruth; David Becomes King

Summary: God promised David a house, a throne, and a kingdom that would last forever. David's sons failed, but the promise did not, for it pointed beyond them to a Son of David who would reign eternally. In Jesus, the Davidic covenant finds its fulfillment and its King.
RelatedEvents: Davidic Covenant; David Becomes King

Summary: The Day of the Lord is the day God steps in decisively — to judge evil, rescue His people, and set the world right. The prophets warned that it would be darkness for the proud and light for the humble, and the New Testament ties it to Christ's return. It is both a warning to the complacent and a hope for the oppressed.

Dependence is not weakness to be outgrown but the truth of the Christian life: apart from Christ we can do nothing. Like branches on a vine, believers draw every good thing from Him — strength, wisdom, and fruit. To depend on God is to live honestly, admitting need and receiving grace.
RelatedEvents: The Temptation in the Wilderness; Jesus Prays in Gethsemane

Summary: Diligence is steady, faithful effort over the long haul — the ant's wisdom, the athlete's discipline, the farmer's patience. Scripture warns against laziness and praises the worker who keeps at the task God has given. Diligence trusts that small, faithful acts compound into a life well lived.
RelatedEvents: Nehemiah Rebuilds the Wall; Rebuilding of the Temple

Summary: Work was given before the Fall, not as punishment but as purpose: to tend, build, and create. Scripture calls believers to work heartily, as for the Lord, whether in fields, workshops, or homes. Diligent work honors God, serves neighbors, and witnesses to a faith that takes ordinary life seriously.
RelatedPeople: Adam; Paul; Joseph, Son of Jacob
RelatedEvents: Creation; Joseph Rises to Power in Egypt

Summary: God sometimes spoke through dreams — to Joseph in Egypt, to Daniel in Babylon, to Joseph the carpenter in Bethlehem. Dreams in Scripture are never treated as private horoscopes; they are tested by God's word and often carry His guidance for others. They remind us that God speaks in ways we do not control, and His messages always serve His purposes.
RelatedPeople: Joseph, Son of Jacob; Daniel; Joseph, Husband of Mary
RelatedEvents: Joseph Sold into Egypt; Joseph Rises to Power in Egypt

Summary: In a valley of dry bones, God asked Ezekiel whether they could live, then breathed life into them by His Spirit. The vision promised Israel's restoration from exile, and it points further to resurrection itself: the God who revives the dead can revive any hopeless situation. No valley is too dry for His breath.
RelatedEvents: Raising of Lazarus; The Resurrection

Summary: Encouragement is a ministry every believer can practice: strengthening hearts, cheering the weary, and reminding one another of God's promises. Barnabas earned the name 'son of encouragement' by standing with new believers and vouching for the unlikely. A word of encouragement can be the difference between quitting and enduring.
RelatedEvents: Pentecost; Paul's Missionary Journeys

Summary: Endurance is staying faithful when faith is costly — under trial, persecution, or long waiting. Hebrews pictures believers surrounded by witnesses, laying aside weights and looking to Jesus, who endured the cross. Endurance is not grim stoicism but hope-fueled perseverance to the finish.
RelatedPeople: Paul; James, Son of Zebedee; Stephen
RelatedEvents: Martyrdom of Stephen; The Crucifixion

Summary: God's gifts are meant to be enjoyed, not merely endured: food, friendship, beauty, rest, and laughter are given by a generous Father. Scripture warns against both idolatry and ingratitude, teaching us to receive good things with thanks and open hands. Enjoyment with thanksgiving is itself a form of worship.
RelatedEvents: Creation; The Feeding of the Five Thousand

Summary: Exile tests faith: far from home, temple, and familiar worship, God's people had to decide whether to compromise or remain faithful. Daniel, Esther, and Mordecai show different faces of that faithfulness — quiet integrity, courageous risk, and prayerful trust. Their stories teach believers living as strangers in a foreign culture how to stand firm without losing love.
RelatedEvents: Daniel in the Lions' Den; Esther Saves Her People

Summary: Faithfulness is loyalty over time — keeping promises when it costs, trusting God when He seems silent, and doing the next right thing. Scripture celebrates it in Daniel, Joseph, and countless unnamed saints, and above all in God Himself, whose faithfulness never fails. To be faithful is to mirror the character of the God we serve.
RelatedPeople: Daniel; Joseph, Son of Jacob; Paul
RelatedEvents: Daniel in the Lions' Den; Joseph Rises to Power in Egypt

Summary: False teachers are an old danger: voices within the church who twist truth for influence, money, or novelty. Scripture tells believers to test every teaching against the apostles' word and to watch the teacher's life as well as their lips. The best defense against false teaching is knowing the true one deeply.
RelatedPeople: Jesus; Simon Peter; John the Apostle
RelatedEvents: Jerusalem Council

Summary: Error is best refuted not by anger but by truth clearly spoken. Paul answered the Galatian agitators with the gospel itself, and the Jerusalem council settled dispute by Scripture and testimony. Refuting false teaching protects the flock and frees those being misled to return to grace.
RelatedEvents: Jerusalem Council; Conversion of Saul (Paul)

Summary: The fear of God is reverent awe before His holiness, majesty, and power — the beginning of wisdom. It is not cringing terror, for the same God who thunders at Sinai invites His people to draw near. Right fear produces obedience, humility, and freedom from every lesser fear.
RelatedEvents: Giving of the Law at Sinai; The Ten Commandments

Summary: To fear the Lord is to live with a constant awareness that God is holy, near, and worthy of obedience. Scripture makes it the foundation of wisdom, the motive for integrity, and the antidote to fearing people. Those who fear the Lord need fear nothing else.
RelatedEvents: The Burning Bush; Giving of the Law at Sinai

Summary: A good start does not guarantee a good finish, and Scripture honors those who endure to the end. Paul, near death, could say he had fought the good fight and kept the faith — not because he was flawless, but because he stayed the course. Finishing well means holding fast to Christ through every season, including the last.
RelatedEvents: Paul in Rome; Paul Shipwrecked on Malta

Summary: Every life is built on something, and Scripture insists the only sure foundation is Christ. Houses built on sand collapse when storms come; those built on His word stand. The church itself rests on the apostles and prophets with Christ as cornerstone, a foundation no flood can move.
RelatedEvents: The Sermon on the Mount; Rebuilding of the Temple

Summary: Freedom in Scripture begins with liberation: Israel freed from Egypt, sinners freed from sin's power. Christ sets people free not to live for themselves but to live for God and neighbor in love. True freedom is not doing whatever we want, but being free at last to do what is right.
RelatedEvents: The Exodus and the Red Sea; The Passover

Summary: Jesus startled His disciples by calling them friends, not merely servants. Friendship with Christ means knowing His mind, sharing His purposes, and enjoying His presence — a relationship of love, not just duty. He proved that friendship by laying down His life for His friends.
RelatedEvents: The Last Supper; The Burning Bush

Summary: The fruit of the Spirit is the character Jesus produces in those who walk with Him: love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, and self-control. It cannot be manufactured by effort alone; it grows as believers abide in Christ. Where the Spirit rules, the fruit appears.
RelatedEvents: Pentecost; The Sermon on the Mount

Summary: Fulfillment is what happens when God's promises land: the Law fulfilled in Christ, the prophets' hopes realized in His coming, death, and resurrection. Jesus did not discard the old story but brought it to its destination. Every promise of God finds its yes in Him.
RelatedEvents: The Resurrection; The Birth of Jesus

Summary: The cross was full payment for sin — not a deposit, not a partial settlement, but a complete satisfaction of God's justice. Hebrews stresses that Christ's one offering perfected forever those being made holy. Because the debt is fully paid, believers stand before God without condemnation and without fear.
RelatedEvents: The Crucifixion; The Passover

Summary: Genealogies are more than lists of names; they are the Bible's way of saying God works through generations. They connect promise to fulfillment, Abraham to David to Jesus, and they include the unexpected — foreigners, failures, and the overlooked. In a genealogy, every name matters because every life is part of the story.
RelatedEvents: Creation; The Call of Abraham

Summary: When Israel stood trapped at the Red Sea, Moses told them to stand still and watch the Lord fight for them. Again and again Scripture shows God as warrior on behalf of His helpless people, winning battles they could never win. The Christian's confidence is the same: the battle belongs to the Lord.
RelatedEvents: The Exodus and the Red Sea; Crossing the Jordan

Summary: God's choice — His election — is His free, gracious decision to set His love on a people who did not earn it. Israel was chosen not for greatness but by grace, and believers are chosen in Christ before the foundation of the world. Election humbles pride and anchors assurance: salvation rests on God's choice, not ours.
RelatedEvents: The Call of Abraham; The Exodus and the Red Sea

Summary: God's faithfulness is the bedrock of every promise: what He says, He does, across centuries and despite human failure. From the exodus to the return from exile to the coming of Christ, His people learned that His word never returns empty. When everything else shifts, His faithfulness holds.
RelatedEvents: The Exodus and the Red Sea; Wilderness Wanderings

Summary: God's glory is the radiant weight of who He is — His holiness, power, and beauty made visible. Moses glimpsed it on the mountain, Isaiah saw it fill the temple, and John saw it made flesh in Jesus. The whole creation exists to display it, and the believer's destiny is to share in it.
RelatedEvents: The Burning Bush; Transfiguration

Summary: Zephaniah dares to say God rejoices over His people with singing. This is not a distant, reluctant love but a Father's delight in His restored children. Even after exile and failure, God celebrates His people's return — a joy the prodigal's father echoes when his lost son comes home.
RelatedEvents: The Prodigal Son; Nehemiah Rebuilds the Wall

Summary: God's justice means He always does what is right: defending the oppressed, judging the wicked, and keeping His world moral. It is good news for victims and a warning for oppressors, for no wrong escapes His notice forever. At the cross, justice and mercy meet: sin is judged, and sinners are saved.
RelatedEvents: Destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah; The Fall

Summary: Mercy is God's compassion toward those who deserve judgment — His steady refusal to give us what our sins have earned. From the golden calf to the prodigal son, Scripture shows mercy triumphing again and again. Those who receive mercy are called to show it.
RelatedEvents: The Golden Calf; The Prodigal Son

Summary: God's presence is His nearness to His people: in the burning bush, in the tabernacle, in Christ Immanuel, and now by His Spirit. It is both comfort and challenge — the presence that guides, corrects, and never leaves. Heaven itself is described as God dwelling with His people forever.
RelatedEvents: The Burning Bush; Pentecost

Summary: God's promises are His word staked on His character, from Abraham's offspring to David's throne to the new covenant. They are not wishes but certainties, kept across generations and fulfilled in Christ. Believers live by trusting promises they have not yet seen fulfilled.
RelatedEvents: The Call of Abraham; Davidic Covenant

Summary: Scripture holds two truths together: God is wrathful toward evil, and He is a refuge for those who flee to Him. The flood, the Passover, and the cross all show the same pattern — judgment falls, and a shelter is provided. To take refuge in God is to be safe from the very wrath He pours out.
RelatedEvents: Noah and the Flood; The Passover

Summary: Godliness is a life shaped by God — reverent, disciplined, and good, trained by grace rather than by rules alone. Paul tells Timothy to train for it like an athlete, because it holds promise for this life and the next. True godliness is visible: it changes how we speak, spend, work, and love.
RelatedEvents: The Sermon on the Mount; Pentecost

Summary: Godly leadership is shepherding, not dominating: feeding, guiding, and protecting those entrusted to your care. Scripture warns leaders against pride and greed, and holds up Moses, Nehemiah, and above all Christ, who led by serving. The measure of a leader is the flourishing of those led.
RelatedEvents: Nehemiah Rebuilds the Wall; The Burning Bush

Summary: Good works do not save, but the saved do good works: they are the fruit of faith, prepared by God for His people to walk in. From the Good Samaritan's mercy to simple daily kindness, good works make the gospel visible. Faith without works is dead; works without faith are empty.
RelatedEvents: The Good Samaritan; The Sermon on the Mount

Summary: Creation is good because its Maker is good: light, land, sea, and creatures were declared good before humanity arrived. The psalms invite us to delight in that goodness, and Paul argues creation itself reveals God's power. Caring for creation and enjoying it are both acts of worship.
RelatedEvents: Creation; Noah and the Flood

Summary: The gospel remakes relationships: enemies reconciled, masters and servants redefined as brothers, marriages and friendships reshaped by grace. Paul's letter to Philemon shows it in miniature — a runaway slave returned as a beloved brother. Where the gospel takes root, relationships change.
RelatedEvents: Jerusalem Council; Pentecost

Summary: Gospel purity means keeping the good news unmixed: Christ plus nothing, grace without add-ons. Paul was fierce on this point, warning that a different gospel is no gospel at all. Purity protects freedom, for anything added to grace becomes a burden.
RelatedEvents: Jerusalem Council; Conversion of Saul (Paul)

Summary: Gratitude is the fitting response to grace: recognizing every good gift as from God's hand and saying so. Scripture commands thanksgiving in all circumstances, not because every circumstance is good, but because God is good in every circumstance. A grateful heart is a worshiping heart.
RelatedEvents: The Last Supper; The Feeding of the Five Thousand

Summary: Grief is honored in Scripture, not hurried past: psalms of lament, Jesus weeping at Lazarus's tomb, and the promise that God will wipe away every tear. Christian grief is real sorrow held alongside real hope — we grieve, but not as those who have no hope. God is near to the brokenhearted.
RelatedPeople: Jesus; King David; Mary of Bethany
RelatedEvents: Raising of Lazarus; The Crucifixion

Summary: Growth is the normal Christian life: from milk to solid food, from seed to harvest, from new birth to maturity. It comes through God's word, prayer, community, and trials, and it is measured less by speed than by direction. The call is simple: keep growing up into Christ.
RelatedEvents: Pentecost; Paul's Missionary Journeys

Summary: Homecoming is the Bible's great arc: exiles returning, prodigals embraced, a people brought back to their God. Ezra's generation rebuilt what was ruined, and Jesus told of a Father who runs to meet a returning son. Every homecoming whispers of the final one, when God brings His people home forever.
RelatedEvents: The Prodigal Son; Cyrus's Decree and Return from Exile

Summary: Hope in suffering is not denial but defiance: the conviction that present pain is not the whole story. Paul argues that suffering produces endurance, endurance character, and character hope — a hope that does not disappoint. The resurrection guarantees that suffering has an end and a purpose.
RelatedEvents: The Resurrection; The Crucifixion

Summary: Hospitality must be guarded as well as generous: Scripture warns against welcoming deceivers and false teachers into the church's trust. Discernment is not the opposite of love but its protection — testing what is taught while keeping the door open to genuine need. Wise welcome loves both truth and neighbor.
RelatedEvents: Jerusalem Council; Peter and Cornelius

Summary: Hospitality is welcoming the stranger as Abraham welcomed travelers and as God welcomed us. It is not about impressive homes but open hearts, tables, and lives. In a world of closed doors, Christian hospitality makes the gospel visible before a word is spoken.
RelatedEvents: The Call of Abraham; Peter and Cornelius

Summary: When the nation fell, God preserved a humble remnant — a small, faithful few who still trusted Him. Elijah thought he was alone; God reminded him of seven thousand who had not bowed. The remnant principle runs through Scripture: God often works through the small and the overlooked.
RelatedEvents: Elijah on Mount Carmel; Fall of Jerusalem and the Exile

Summary: Identity in Christ answers the question of who we are: new creations, children of God, members of His body, citizens of heaven. It replaces identities built on achievement, ancestry, or approval with one given by grace. To know who you are in Christ is to know what you are for.
RelatedEvents: Conversion of Saul (Paul); The Baptism of Jesus

Summary: Inheritance is what God's children receive as His heirs: a kingdom, a new creation, and God Himself as their portion. Israel's land was a down payment; the full inheritance awaits Christ's return, incorruptible and unfading. Believers live now as heirs, already rich and not yet home.
RelatedEvents: Crossing the Jordan; The Resurrection

Summary: The gospel is an invitation, not an ultimatum: come, all who are thirsty; come to the feast; come to Me, all who labor. Isaiah, Jesus, and Revelation all sound the same open call to anyone who will hear. The church's task is to keep issuing that invitation with warmth and urgency.
RelatedEvents: The Sermon on the Mount; The Feeding of the Five Thousand

Summary: Israel's identity was given, not earned: chosen by God, set apart as His treasured possession, and called to be a light to the nations. That identity survived slavery, wilderness, and exile because it rested on God's choice, not Israel's performance. In Christ, the church inherits that calling as God's people.
RelatedEvents: The Exodus and the Red Sea; Giving of the Law at Sinai

Summary: After judgment came restoration: dry bones lived, exiles returned, and the temple rose again. Restoration was never merely political; it was God renewing His covenant and His people from within. The prophets' vision points beyond return from Babylon to the new covenant and the new creation.
RelatedEvents: Cyrus's Decree and Return from Exile; Rebuilding of the Temple

Summary: Joy in hardship sounds impossible until you see Paul singing in prison or Habakkuk rejoicing with no harvest in sight. Christian joy does not depend on circumstances but on Christ, who is present in them. It is a stubborn gladness that suffering cannot cancel.
RelatedEvents: Paul Shipwrecked on Malta; Martyrdom of Stephen

Summary: Judgment and mercy meet in God's character: He judges sin truly and forgives sinners freely. The psalmist says mercy and truth meet together, and James warns that mercy triumphs over judgment for the merciful. At the cross both are fully satisfied — sin condemned, sinners welcomed.
RelatedEvents: The Golden Calf; Destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah

Summary: False teachers face a severe judgment, Scripture warns, because they lead others astray while claiming God's name. Peter and Jude describe their end soberly, not gleefully — as a warning to the church to guard the truth. The severity of the judgment matches the seriousness of the trust betrayed.
RelatedPeople: Simon Peter; John the Apostle; Jesus
RelatedEvents: Jerusalem Council

Summary: Nineveh repented at Jonah's preaching, but a century later Nahum announced its fall: a city that returned to violence would face God's judgment. Nineveh's story warns that repentance must be real and lasting, and that no empire, however great, stands outside God's justice.
RelatedEvents: Jonah and Nineveh; Jonah and the Great Fish

Summary: Pride invites judgment because it claims God's place: Babel's tower, Nebuchadnezzar's boast, and every heart that exalts itself. God humbles the proud not out of cruelty but to restore truth — that He alone is great. The humbled, by contrast, are lifted up.
RelatedEvents: The Tower of Babel

Summary: Justification by faith is the heart of the gospel: sinners are declared righteous before God not by works but by trusting Christ. Abraham believed and it was credited to him as righteousness, and the same faith credits righteousness to all who believe. Justification is a gift received, never a wage earned.
RelatedEvents: The Call of Abraham; The Crucifixion

Summary: Kingdom living is life under God's reign here and now: seeking His kingdom first, practicing its values of mercy, purity, and peacemaking. It is not waiting for heaven but inhabiting heaven's rule on earth, in homes, workplaces, and neighborhoods. The Sermon on the Mount is its charter.
RelatedEvents: The Sermon on the Mount; Pentecost

Summary: Matthew's phrase 'kingdom of heaven' describes God's reign breaking into the world through Jesus. It arrives quietly — like seed, yeast, and treasure — yet it overturns every other allegiance. To enter it is to submit to the King and receive a citizenship that outlasts every earthly kingdom.
RelatedEvents: The Baptism of Jesus; The Sermon on the Mount

Summary: Scripture contrasts the kingdoms of this world — built on power, wealth, and pride — with the kingdom of God, which lasts forever. Empires rise and fall, from Babel to Rome, but Daniel saw a kingdom that would never be destroyed. Believers live as citizens of the lasting kingdom while sojourning in temporary ones.
RelatedEvents: The Tower of Babel; Daniel in the Lions' Den

Summary: Christ's kingship was proclaimed at His birth, mocked at His trial, and vindicated at His resurrection. He reigns now from heaven, and He will return to reign openly, every knee bowing before Him. To confess Jesus as Lord is to pledge allegiance to the true King.
RelatedEvents: Triumphal Entry; The Resurrection

Summary: Kingship belongs to God: the psalms call Him King over all the earth, and Israel's kings were meant to rule as His deputies. Human kingship failed again and again, which is why the promise of a perfect King mattered so much. All authority is borrowed; only God's kingship is absolute.
RelatedEvents: David Becomes King; Triumphal Entry

Summary: Knowledge of Christ is not mere information about Him but a living acquaintance that transforms. Paul counted everything loss beside knowing Christ, and Peter urges believers to grow in that knowledge. To know Him is eternal life, and it deepens through Scripture, prayer, and obedience.
RelatedEvents: Transfiguration; Conversion of Saul (Paul)

Summary: Language is a gift that builds and breaks: it confused Babel, united Pentecost, and daily shapes communities. Scripture warns that the tongue is a small fire with great power, and calls believers to speak truth with grace. How we use words reveals what rules our hearts.
RelatedEvents: The Tower of Babel; Pentecost

Summary: Living faith is faith with hands and feet: trusting God and acting on that trust, as Abraham did when he left home and Rahab did when she hid the spies. James insists that faith without works is dead — not because works save, but because real trust always moves. Living faith obeys, gives, forgives, and goes.
RelatedEvents: The Call of Abraham; The Walls of Jericho

Summary: Living hope is hope made alive by Christ's resurrection — not wishful thinking but confident expectation of an inheritance kept in heaven. Peter writes to suffering believers that this hope guards them through trials and purifies them for glory. It is called living because it grows, endures, and changes how we live today.
RelatedEvents: The Resurrection; Pentecost

Summary: Love for God is the first and greatest commandment: to love Him with all heart, soul, mind, and strength. It is not sentiment alone but loyalty shown in obedience, worship, and trust. We love because He first loved us, and that love spills over to every neighbor.
RelatedEvents: The Sermon on the Mount; The Last Supper

Summary: God's majesty is his royal splendor: the weight of glory that makes mountains tremble and angels cover their faces. Scripture clothes him in light, seats him above the flood, and crowns him with honor no creature can rival. To behold his majesty is both to tremble and to trust, for the majestic God is also the shepherd who carries his lambs close to his heart.
RelatedEvents: Transfiguration

Summary: Marriage in Scripture is a covenant, not merely a contract: a solemn, lifelong bond in which husband and wife become one flesh and mirror God's faithful love for his people. Genesis gives its pattern, the prophets use it to picture God's covenant with Israel, and Paul lifts it higher still as a picture of Christ and the church. Guarding marriage therefore guards a living sermon about God's keeping love.

Life's meaning is the question Ecclesiastes presses hardest: what lasts, what satisfies, what makes the brief years under the sun worth living? Apart from God, even wisdom, wealth, and work turn to vapor; with him, ordinary days gain weight and purpose. Scripture's answer is not a technique but a Person: we are made by God, for God, and find our meaning in fearing him, keeping his commandments, and enjoying his gifts as from his hand.

Israel waited for a Messiah: an anointed king from David's line who would defeat God's enemies and reign in righteousness. Jesus is that King, though his crown came by a cross and his throne by resurrection. He reigns now over all things for the good of his church, and one day every knee will bow to him.
RelatedEvents: Triumphal Entry; The Crucifixion; The Resurrection

Summary: Long before Jesus came, God's people lived on promises: a seed who would crush the serpent, a son of David whose kingdom would never end, a suffering servant who would bear our griefs. That hope sustained exiles, prophets, and ordinary families through centuries of waiting. In Jesus the hope arrived, and because he rose, our hope now looks forward to his return and the renewal of all things.
RelatedEvents: The Birth of Jesus; The Resurrection

Summary: God is not far off: he draws near to the brokenhearted, dwells with the humble, and invites his people to draw near in return. The tabernacle, the temple, and finally the incarnation all tell one story: God closing the distance sin created. James promises simply that if we draw near to God, he will draw near to us, and Psalm 73 confesses that the nearness of God is our good.
RelatedEvents: The Burning Bush

Summary: After the judges' cycles of failure, Israel cried out for a king, and God gave them first Saul, then David, teaching them that no human king could finally save. The longing itself was right: God's people need a righteous ruler to lead them in God's ways and defend them from their enemies. That need is answered only in Jesus, the King whose reign brings justice without tyranny and victory without violence.
RelatedPeople: Samuel; King Saul; King David; Jesus
RelatedEvents: Anointing of Saul as King; David Becomes King

Summary: God promised through Jeremiah a covenant written on hearts, not stone, with sins forgiven and God known personally. Jesus inaugurated it at the Last Supper, saying the cup is the new covenant in his blood. We live under it now: forgiven, indwelt by the Spirit, and called to a new life of obedience from the inside out.
RelatedEvents: Last Supper; The Crucifixion; Pentecost

Summary: God promised through Ezekiel to remove hearts of stone and give hearts of flesh, writing his law within and putting his Spirit in his people. A new heart is not self-improvement but resurrection: God replaces rebellion with responsiveness, so that we love what he loves and turn from what we once loved. This is the inward miracle behind every true conversion and every lasting change.
RelatedEvents: Pentecost; The Conversion of Paul

Summary: Faithfulness in Scripture almost always meets opposition: Nehemiah's wall-builders held a trowel in one hand and a sword in the other, Daniel's enemies plotted against his prayers, and the apostles were ordered to stop speaking in Jesus' name. Opposition is not a sign that God has abandoned his work; often it is the sign that the work matters. God's people answer it with prayer, courage, and steady obedience, trusting the Lord who builds what no enemy can tear down.
RelatedEvents: Nehemiah Rebuilds the Wall; Martyrdom of Stephen

Summary: At Pentecost the promised Spirit fell like wind and fire, filling ordinary disciples with boldness to speak of Jesus in every tongue. The outpouring Joel foresaw had come: sons and daughters prophesying, old men dreaming dreams, God's presence poured out on all flesh. The same Spirit still fills the church today, giving gifts for service and power for witness until Christ returns.
RelatedEvents: Pentecost

Summary: God's work has always been shared work: Paul and Barnabas, Priscilla and Aquila, Paul and Timothy, partners in the gospel bound by affection, trust, and a common mission. Partnership is more than efficiency; it is the shape of the body of Christ, where gifts differ and burdens are carried together. Even the strongest leaders in Scripture leaned on companions, reminding us that ministry done alone is ministry done wrong.
RelatedEvents: Paul's Missionary Journeys

Summary: A plea is prayer at its most honest: an urgent cry for mercy, help, or deliverance when we have nothing left to offer. The psalms are full of pleas: How long, O Lord? And Jesus honored the blind beggar's plea, Son of David, have mercy on me. God does not despise a pleading heart; he bends his ear to it, and often the plea itself is the beginning of faith.
RelatedEvents: Jesus Calms the Storm

Summary: Praise is God's people answering his goodness with song, speech, and shouting joy. The Psalms model it in every season: praise rises from deliverance, from creation's beauty, and even from the depths. Praise is both a gift we offer and a weapon against despair, because it fixes our eyes on who God is rather than on what we fear.

God's preservation is his keeping power: he guarded Noah through the flood, kept a remnant in exile, and preserves his people to the end. Jude calls believers kept for Jesus Christ, and Jesus promised that no one can snatch his sheep from his hand. Preservation is not immunity from hardship but security through it: God keeps what is his, and he will finish what he began.
RelatedEvents: Noah and the Flood

Summary: In the Old Testament, priests stood between God and his people, offering sacrifices and blessing in God's name; Aaron and his sons carried this holy, costly calling. The New Testament announces a better priesthood: Jesus, our great high priest, offered himself once for all, and now all believers are a royal priesthood with direct access to God. We no longer need a human mediator, because the Mediator lives forever to intercede for us.
RelatedEvents: The Crucifixion

Summary: Life is short and demands are endless, so Scripture urges us to choose what matters first: God's kingdom, his people, and the work he has actually given us. Martha learned that one thing is necessary; Mary chose the good portion at Jesus' feet. Right priorities are not found by doing more but by seeking first what God seeks, and letting the rest find its place beneath it.
RelatedPeople: Jesus; Martha; Mary of Bethany; Paul

Summary: Prophets were God's mouthpieces, speaking his word to kings and crowds whether they wanted to hear it or not. Their witness combined courage and compassion: denouncing injustice and idolatry while holding out mercy to all who would turn. The church inherits that calling: to speak truth in love, to name sin honestly, and to testify to Jesus, for the testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy.
RelatedPeople: Jeremiah; Amos; Micah; John the Apostle
RelatedEvents: Elijah on Mount Carmel; Jonah and Nineveh

Summary: The prophets were men and women God called to speak his word into their times: Moses the lawgiver, Samuel the kingmaker, Elijah the firebrand, Isaiah the seer, and John the Baptist, the last and greatest of the old order. They comforted the afflicted and afflicted the comfortable, always pointing beyond themselves to the coming Messiah. Their books still preach, because the God who spoke through them has not stopped speaking.
RelatedPeople: Moses; Samuel; Elijah; Isaiah; John the Baptist
RelatedEvents: Elijah on Mount Carmel; The Burning Bush

Summary: Purity is singleness of heart: a life unmixed, undivided, and set apart for God. Jesus promised that the pure in heart will see God, and the New Testament calls believers to flee impurity and to wash in the truth that makes us clean. Purity is not prudishness but wholeness: the same God who made our bodies calls us to honor him in them, by the power of the Spirit who dwells within.

Rebellion is the old human story: creatures shaking their fists at the Creator, from Eden's forbidden tree to Israel's golden calf to our own daily refusals. Scripture never softens it: rebellion brings ruin. Yet it never leaves it hopeless, for God answers rebellion with mercy, pursuing rebels until they come home. Every story of rebellion in the Bible is therefore also a story about grace that is greater than our defiance.
RelatedEvents: The Fall; The Golden Calf

Summary: Rebuilding is God's repeated work among ruins: after judgment, after exile, after failure, he gathers what is broken and builds again. Nehemiah rebuilt a wall, Zerubbabel a temple, and God himself rebuilds ruined lives, raising them into a holy temple in the Lord. The Bible's rebuilding stories teach us not to despise small beginnings, for God delights to start again with what the world calls wreckage.
RelatedEvents: Nehemiah Rebuilds the Wall; Rebuilding of the Temple

Summary: When trouble comes, Scripture invites us to run to God as to a fortress, a shelter, a hiding place. The psalmists call him refuge in war, in grief, in guilt, and in old age: not a distant idea but a present help. To take refuge in God is to trust his character more than our circumstances, and to hide in him until the storm passes.

Remembering is a spiritual discipline in Scripture, not mere nostalgia: Israel was commanded to remember the Exodus, to retell it to their children, and to set up stones so they would not forget. Forgetting God is the first step toward idolatry; remembering his deeds is the anchor of faith in every new crisis. The Lord's Supper is remembering made tangible: bread and cup that preach the gospel to our forgetful hearts.
RelatedEvents: The Passover; Last Supper; The Exodus and Crossing of the Red Sea

Summary: Remembrance in the Bible is active: God remembers his covenant, and his people are called to remember his works, his words, and his warnings. Memorials: Passover, the stones at Gilgal, the Lord's Supper, were given because human hearts drift. To remember rightly is to live gratefully and obediently, letting yesterday's deliverances fuel today's trust.
RelatedEvents: The Passover; Crossing the Jordan; Last Supper

Summary: Again and again God preserves a remnant: a faithful few kept through judgment: Noah's family, the seven thousand who never bowed to Baal, the exiles who returned. The remnant is proof that God's purposes never depend on majorities, and that his grace always keeps a people for himself. In the New Testament the remnant widens: Jews and Gentiles together, chosen by grace, become the one people of God.
RelatedEvents: Elijah on Mount Carmel; Cyrus's Decree and Return from Exile

Summary: After seventy years in Babylon, God kept his promise and brought his people home: Cyrus decreed it, Zerubbabel led it, and Ezra and Nehemiah rebuilt what exile had broken. The return was joyful yet incomplete: the people were home but still waiting for a greater deliverance. That longing points to Christ, whose return from the grave and promised return in glory will end every exile for good.
RelatedPeople: Cyrus the Great; Zerubbabel; Ezra; Nehemiah
RelatedEvents: Cyrus's Decree and Return from Exile; Ezra Reads the Law; Nehemiah Rebuilds the Wall

Summary: The New Testament ends as it begins its hope: Jesus, who ascended, will return in glory to judge the living and the dead and to make all things new. His return is not a puzzle to solve but a promise to live by: it calls us to readiness, to holiness, and to hope that no suffering is final. Every Maranatha since the apostles has been the church's way of saying: come, Lord Jesus.
RelatedEvents: The Ascension; The Resurrection

Summary: Return is the Bible's word for repentance: turning back from the far country to the Father, from idols to the living God. The prodigal's return is the pattern: a long walk home met by a running father. God does not merely permit return; he pleads for it, promises to receive it, and rejoices over every sinner who turns.
RelatedEvents: The Prodigal Son; The Conversion of Paul

Summary: The Bible is full of reunions that picture God's heart: Jacob embracing Esau, Joseph revealing himself to his brothers, the father running to his prodigal son. Each reunion is a small resurrection: what was lost is found, what was dead is alive. The greatest reunion is still to come, when God's scattered people are gathered from every nation to one table with the Lamb.
RelatedPeople: Jacob; Esau; Joseph, Son of Jacob; Jesus
RelatedEvents: Joseph and His Brothers; The Prodigal Son

Summary: God delights in reversals: the last become first, the proud are scattered, the humble lifted, the cross becomes a throne. Hannah sang it, Mary sang it, and Jesus lived it: the stone the builders rejected became the cornerstone. Reversal is the gospel's logic: God saves by turning the world's values upside down, so that no one can boast except in the Lord.
RelatedPeople: Hannah; Mary, Mother of Jesus; Jesus; Paul
RelatedEvents: The Crucifixion; The Resurrection

Summary: The righteousness of God is both who he is and what he does: he is perfectly just, and he acts to make things right, vindicating the oppressed and judging the wicked. In the gospel, Paul announces something astonishing: God's righteousness is given to sinners through faith in Christ, so that the unjust are declared just. To trust in God's righteousness is to stop building our own and to rest in his finished work.
RelatedEvents: The Crucifixion; The Resurrection

Summary: David rose from shepherd boy to king: anointed in obscurity, tested in the wilderness, crowned after years of waiting and war. His rise shows God's pattern of choosing the overlooked and preparing leaders in hidden places. Yet David's story also warns us: the king after God's own heart fell grievously, and his greater Son would be the King who never falls.
RelatedPeople: Samuel; King David; King Saul; Jonathan
RelatedEvents: David Becomes King; David and Goliath

Summary: The good news is not for one tribe or nation: Simeon called Jesus a light for the Gentiles, the angels announced joy for all people, and Revelation pictures a multitude from every nation before the throne. God desires all people to be saved, and the church's mission flows from that breadth: a Savior for all means a gospel for all.
RelatedEvents: The Birth of Jesus; Pentecost

Summary: The servant theme runs from Joseph and Moses through Isaiah's suffering servant to Jesus, who came not to be served but to serve and give his life as a ransom. True greatness in God's kingdom is measured by towel and basin, not throne and title. To follow the Servant is to take the lowest place gladly, trusting that the Father sees and rewards what the world overlooks.
RelatedEvents: Last Supper; The Crucifixion

Summary: Service is worship with its sleeves rolled up: the church's gifts are given not for display but for building others up, and Jesus made himself the model by washing feet. From deacons to door-keepers, from hosts to helpers, every act of service in Christ's name is sacred work. The New Testament measures spiritual maturity not by knowledge alone but by love that stoops to serve.
RelatedEvents: Last Supper

Summary: To shelter in Christ is to hide in the safest place in the universe: united to him, we are covered by his righteousness, kept by his power, and held through every storm. The psalmist's fortress and the hen's wings both point here: to a refuge that is a person, not a place. Whatever threatens, the believer can say with Paul that nothing can separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord.
RelatedEvents: The Crucifixion; The Resurrection

Summary: Sin is missing God's mark, in thought, word, and deed, and repentance is turning from it back to him, with sorrow for the sin and trust in his mercy. Scripture never separates the two: conviction without repentance hardens, and repentance without conviction is shallow. The good news is that God grants repentance as a gift, and every turning sinner finds a Father ready to forgive.
RelatedEvents: The Prodigal Son; The Crucifixion

Summary: Social righteousness is God's justice lived out in public: defending the widow, feeding the hungry, freeing the oppressed, and ordering society by mercy and truth. The prophets thundered against courts that favored the rich and worship that ignored the poor, because God cares how neighbors treat neighbors. The church practices social righteousness when it serves its city, advocates for the vulnerable, and shows the world what God's kingdom looks like.
RelatedEvents: The Good Samaritan; The Sermon on the Mount

Summary: Son of God is the New Testament's great confession about Jesus: he is not merely a prophet or teacher but God's own Son, sharing the Father's nature and authority. The title rings out at his baptism, in Peter's confession, on the cross from a Roman centurion, and in John's Gospel from first verse to last. To call Jesus the Son of God is to worship him and to trust that in him we meet God himself.
RelatedPeople: Jesus; Simon Peter; John the Baptist
RelatedEvents: The Baptism of Jesus; The Crucifixion

Summary: Son of Man was Jesus' favorite name for himself, drawn from Daniel's vision of one like a son of man coming with the clouds to receive an everlasting kingdom. In Jesus the title holds both glory and suffering together: the Son of Man has authority to forgive sins, came to seek and save the lost, and must be lifted up like the serpent in the wilderness. To confess him as Son of Man is to confess a King who rules by laying down his life.
RelatedEvents: The Crucifixion; Transfiguration

Summary: Sound doctrine is teaching that is healthy: true to Scripture, centered on Christ, and producing godly lives. Paul urged Timothy to hold the pattern of sound words and to guard the deposit, because what we believe shapes how we live and whom we trust. False teaching spreads like disease; sound doctrine nourishes, steadies, and protects the church.

Our words reveal our hearts: Scripture warns that the tongue is a small fire able to bless or burn, and it calls us to speech that is truthful, gracious, and seasonable. James pictures the tongue as a rudder steering a whole life, while Proverbs treasures the apt word spoken at the right time. Guarding our speech is therefore not politeness but discipleship: learning to speak as people who will answer to God for every careless word.

The Holy Spirit gives every believer gifts for the common good: wisdom, teaching, encouragement, generosity, leadership, mercy, and more. Paul insists these gifts differ by design, like parts of one body, and that the greatest gift of all is love, without which every other gift is noise. Gifts are not badges of importance but tools of service, to be used humbly, eagerly, and for the building up of the church.
RelatedEvents: Pentecost

Summary: Standing firm is holding your ground when faith is pressured: Paul told the Ephesians to put on God's armor and stand, and told the Corinthians to stand firm in the faith and be strong. Firmness is not stubbornness but rootedness: planted deep in truth, steadied by prayer, and supported by brothers and sisters who stand beside you. The one who stands firm to the end, Jesus promised, will be saved.
RelatedEvents: Martyrdom of Stephen; Daniel in the Lions' Den

Summary: God's strength shows up most clearly where ours runs out: Paul pleaded three times for his thorn to go, and heard, My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness. Weakness is therefore not the enemy of ministry but its doorway, because it forces us to lean on Christ instead of ourselves. The cross is the pattern: apparent defeat that became the world's salvation.
RelatedEvents: The Crucifixion; The Resurrection

Summary: God's sufficiency is his all-enough-ness: he is enough for every need, every trial, and every calling, and his grace never runs short. Paul learned contentment in plenty and in want because he knew the God who supplies; the psalmist found that the Lord is his shepherd and therefore he lacks nothing. Sufficiency does not mean we never feel need: it means our need drives us to the One who is more than enough.
RelatedEvents: Feeding of the Five Thousand

Summary: Hebrews argues from first to last that Jesus is superior: superior to angels, to Moses, to Aaron's priesthood, and to every sacrifice that came before. He is the radiance of God's glory and the exact imprint of his nature, the mediator of a better covenant with better promises. To see Christ's superiority is to stop drifting back to shadows and to hold fast to the substance who is Christ himself.
RelatedEvents: The Crucifixion; Transfiguration

Summary: Ministry has always depended on supporters: the women who funded Jesus' travels from their own means, the Philippians who partnered with Paul again and again, the churches that sent and sustained missionaries. Support, in prayer, in money, in hospitality, in encouragement, is not secondary to ministry; it IS ministry, sharing in the work and its reward. To support gospel work generously is to invest in treasure that outlasts every market.
RelatedEvents: Paul's Missionary Journeys

Summary: Christ is supreme over all things: the firstborn of creation, the head of the church, the one in whom all things hold together and through whom all things will be reconciled. Colossians answers every rival power, philosophy, angel-worship, religious rules, with a single word: Christ is enough, and Christ is first. To live under his supremacy is to give him first place in everything, from our calendars to our ambitions.
RelatedEvents: The Resurrection; The Ascension

Summary: Surrender is yielding our wills, plans, and very lives to God, trusting that his wisdom is better than our control. Mary answered the angel, Let it be to me according to your word; Jesus prayed in Gethsemane, Not my will, but yours. Surrender is not defeat but freedom: the daily laying down of our crowns before the King who gave himself for us.
RelatedEvents: Jesus Prays in Gethsemane; The Crucifixion

Summary: After exile, God stirred Zerubbabel, Joshua, and the returned remnant to rebuild his house in Jerusalem, and later Nehemiah to rebuild its wall. The work faced opposition, delay, and discouragement, yet God promised that the glory of the latter house would be greater than the former. The rebuilt temple pointed forward to Christ, in whom God dwells with his people, and to the church as his living temple.
RelatedEvents: Rebuilding of the Temple; Nehemiah Rebuilds the Wall; Cyrus's Decree and Return from Exile

Summary: Time is God's gift and God's stewardship: brief as a breath, yet long enough to know him, love our neighbors, and finish the work he gives. Scripture urges us to number our days, to redeem the time, and to remember that there is a season for everything under heaven. Eternity gives time its weight: because forever is real, today matters more, not less.

Tithing is giving the first tenth to God, a practice that taught Israel to trust the Lord as provider and to fund the work of worship and the care of the poor. Abraham gave a tenth to Melchizedek and Jacob vowed one long before the law commanded it. Under the new covenant, the tenth remains a wise starting point, but the deeper principle is larger still: generous, cheerful, firstfruits giving from hearts that know everything belongs to God.

Unfaithfulness is breaking trust with God: Israel's idolatry is pictured as adultery, and Hosea's marriage became a living parable of a people who kept wandering from their faithful Husband. Scripture names unfaithfulness plainly because it wounds real relationship. Yet it never ends there, for God remains faithful even when we are faithless, and calls his people back with cords of love.
RelatedEvents: The Golden Calf

Summary: Unity in Christ is deeper than agreement: in him, Jew and Gentile, slave and free, male and female are one people, reconciled to God and to each other by one cross. The dividing wall is broken down, and former strangers become fellow citizens and members of God's household. To live this unity is to refuse every identity that competes with Christ and to love across every line the world draws.
RelatedEvents: Pentecost; Peter and Cornelius

Summary: Unity is the church's witness: Jesus prayed that his people would be one as he and the Father are one, so that the world would believe. Paul pleaded for one mind, one Spirit, one body: not uniformity, for gifts differ, but a deep oneness rooted in one Lord, one faith, one baptism. Unity is kept by humility, gentleness, and forgiveness, and it is broken most often by pride.
RelatedEvents: Pentecost; Jerusalem Council

Summary: Urgency runs through the gospel: now is the day of salvation, the night is far gone, the harvest is plentiful and the workers are few. Jesus warned against the rich fool who planned for tomorrow and lost today, and Paul pleaded with people to be reconciled to God without delay. Urgency is not panic but holy seriousness: living as people who know time is short and eternity is long.

Vanity is the emptiness Ecclesiastes names: chasing wealth, pleasure, wisdom, or fame apart from God leaves the hands full of wind. The Preacher tried everything and found it vapor: beautiful, brief, and unable to satisfy. Vanity is not a counsel of despair but a diagnosis: only when we stop expecting the world to give us meaning can we receive life as God's gift and enjoy it without worshipping it.

Christ's victory was won where defeat seemed certain: on the cross he disarmed the powers, in the tomb he broke death's grip, and in his resurrection he announced that the war is over even while battles remain. Believers share that victory now, over sin, over fear, over the accuser, and will see it complete when he returns. To live in his victory is to fight from triumph, not for it.
RelatedEvents: The Crucifixion; The Resurrection

Summary: Visions are one way God has spoken: Jacob's ladder, Isaiah's throne room, Ezekiel's valley of dry bones, John's apocalypse. They come in pictures because some truths are too large for plain prose, and they always serve God's purposes: calling, comforting, or commissioning his people. Visions must be tested by Scripture and by their fruit, for not every dazzling sight is from God, but the true ones have steadied his people for millennia.
RelatedPeople: Jacob; Isaiah; Ezekiel; John the Apostle
RelatedEvents: Transfiguration

Summary: Waiting on God is active trust, not passive resignation: the psalmist waits more than watchmen for the morning, Isaiah promises new strength to those who wait, and the church waited ten days in prayer before Pentecost. Waiting purifies our motives, deepens our dependence, and teaches us that God's timing is part of his goodness. Those who wait on the Lord will not be put to shame.
RelatedEvents: Pentecost

Summary: Wandering and return is the shape of Israel's story and of every human heart: God's people strayed into the wilderness, into exile, into idolatry, and God kept bringing them back. The wilderness wanderings taught dependence, the exile taught humility, and every return taught grace. Our own wanderings need not end in ruin, because the God who sought Israel still seeks wanderers today.
RelatedEvents: Wilderness Wanderings; The Prodigal Son; Cyrus's Decree and Return from Exile

Summary: The wilderness is where God forms his people: Israel wandered there forty years, Elijah fled there in despair, and Jesus was tested there before his ministry began. It is a place of hunger and danger, but also of manna, of water from the rock, and of God's voice in the silence. No one chooses the wilderness, yet Scripture insists that God meets us there, and leads us out, humbled, fed, and ready.
RelatedEvents: Wilderness Wanderings; The Temptation in the Wilderness

Summary: Works in Scripture are both warned against and commanded: we are not saved by works, yet we are saved for good works, created in Christ Jesus to walk in them. Paul and James agree: faith without works is dead, and works without faith are empty. Good works are therefore not the price of salvation but its fruit: the visible life of a people already loved, already forgiven, already free.
RelatedEvents: The Sermon on the Mount
